field.note: The paragraph restates B12's §Radiocarbon dating ¶2 word for word in its first three sentences; one lineage (F68 under F63).

F1.quote: Determining by means of palaeography the chronology of ancient handwritten manuscripts such as the Dead Sea Scrolls is essential for reconstructing the evolution of ideas, but there is an almost complete lack of date-bearing manuscripts.
F1.claim: the study's problem: palaeographic dating of the scrolls is essential to the history of ideas, and there are almost no date-bearing manuscripts
F1.lineage: the dating problem: palaeography without date-bearing manuscripts

F2.quote: To overcome this problem, we present Enoch, an AI-based date-prediction model, trained on the basis of 24 14 C-dated scroll samples.
F2.claim: the study's definition of its object: Enoch, an AI-based date-prediction model trained on 24 radiocarbon-dated scroll samples
F2.lineage: what it is: an AI-based date-prediction model for the scrolls and the study that introduces it

F3.quote: By applying Bayesian ridge regression on angular and allographic writing style feature vectors, Enoch could predict 14 C-based dates with varied mean absolute errors (MAEs) of 27.9 to 30.7 years.
F3.claim: by Bayesian ridge regression on angular and allographic writing-style features, Enoch predicts the radiocarbon-based dates with mean absolute errors of 27.9 to 30.7 years
F3.lineage: accuracy and validation: errors of 27.9 to 30.7 years; 79% realistic on 135 undated scrolls

F4.quote: In order to explore the viability of the character-shape based dating approach, the trained Enoch model then computed date predictions for 135 non-dated scrolls, aligning with 79% in palaeographic post-hoc evaluation.
F4.claim: to explore the approach's viability, the trained model dated 135 undated scrolls, 79% of its predictions aligning in a palaeographic post-hoc evaluation
F4.lineage: accuracy and validation: errors of 27.9 to 30.7 years; 79% realistic on 135 undated scrolls

F5.quote: The 14 C ranges and Enoch’s style-based predictions are often older than traditionally assumed palaeographic estimates, leading to a new chronology of the scrolls and the re-dating of ancient Jewish key texts that contribute to current debates on Jewish and Christian origins.
F5.claim: the radiocarbon ranges and Enoch's predictions are often older than the palaeographic estimates, giving a new chronology and the re-dating of key texts in debates on Jewish and Christian origins
F5.lineage: the finding: dates older than the palaeographic estimates, a new chronology

F6.quote: Palaeography—the study of ancient handwriting—is used to date manuscripts on the basis of their handwriting [ 2 – 4 ] but its subjectivity and the impossibility of measuring the significance of handwriting features poses a problem [ 5 , 6 ].
F6.claim: palaeography dates manuscripts by their handwriting, and its subjectivity and unmeasurable features are a problem (refs 2–4: Nongbri on early Christian codices; Orsini; Orsini and Clarysse on early New Testament manuscripts)
F6.lineage: the dating problem: palaeography without date-bearing manuscripts

F7.quote: Enoch, named after the ancient Jewish science hero, was trained as a machine-learning-based date-prediction model applying Bayesian ridge regression on established handwriting-style descriptors.
F7.claim: the model is named after the ancient Jewish science hero, and trained as a machine-learning date-prediction model on handwriting-style descriptors
F7.lineage: reception: the encyclopedia and the name

F8.quote: Thus, Enoch reduces palaeographic subjectivity and the role of implicit knowledge by offering date predictions as probability-based options, grounded in physical ( 14 C) and geometric (shape-based) evidences, that can aid palaeographers and historians in their decision-making and contribute to historical debates.
F8.claim: Enoch reduces palaeographic subjectivity by offering dates as probability-based options grounded in radiocarbon and shape-based evidence, to aid palaeographers and historians
F8.lineage: what it offers palaeography: probability-based options, quantified objectivity, explainable design

F9.quote: We performed 14 C dating on 30 manuscripts from 4 sites, spanning an estimated 5 centuries … The AMS results yielded 27 valid 14 C dates
F9.claim: the team radiocarbon-dated 30 manuscripts from four sites spanning about five centuries; 27 dates were valid
F9.lineage: the radiocarbon anchors: 30 manuscripts dated, 27 valid dates, 24 for training

F10.quote: Sample 4Q114 is one of the most significant findings of the 14 C results. … The accepted 2 calibrated range for 4Q114, 230–160 BCE, overlaps with the period in which the final part of the biblical book of Daniel was presumably authored
F10.claim: 4Q114 (Daniel 8–11) is a radiocarbon result: its range, 230–160 BCE, overlaps the period in which the end of Daniel was presumably written
F10.lineage: the key texts: 4Q114 by radiocarbon, 4Q109 by Enoch, copies from the time of their presumed authors

F11.quote: We used 24 manuscripts from the 14 C samples with valid dates as a labeled dataset for the primary training set for Enoch
F11.claim: 24 of the radiocarbon-dated manuscripts are the model's primary training set
F11.lineage: the radiocarbon anchors: 30 manuscripts dated, 27 valid dates, 24 for training

F12.quote: It was decided to let the available data speak, not depending on a pre-trained model
F12.claim: no pre-trained model: only the scrolls' own data trains the predictor
F12.lineage: the method: Bayesian ridge regression on writing-style features read from the ink trace, not the text

F13.quote: In this study, ‘style’ is not related to textual content or wording.
F13.claim: the study's definition of style: shapes along the ink trace, unrelated to the text's content or wording
F13.lineage: the method: Bayesian ridge regression on writing-style features read from the ink trace, not the text

F14.quote: The feature vectors relate directly to the shape-based evidence of the ink traces in the manuscripts and have a solid basis in writer identification [ 28 – 30 ] and document dating [ 31 , 32 ].
F14.claim: the features come from the ink traces and rest on writer identification and document dating
F14.lineage: the method: Bayesian ridge regression on writing-style features read from the ink trace, not the text

F15.quote: 14 C date ranges are evidently superior to style-based predictions.
F15.claim: the study's own limit: radiocarbon ranges are superior to the style-based predictions
F15.lineage: stated limits: radiocarbon superior, a first step, more research needed

F16.quote: For Ithaca [ 39 ], AI and epigraphy were similarly used as two heterogeneous information sources to predict dates for ancient Greek inscriptions.
F16.claim: the study sets Enoch beside Ithaca, which combined AI and epigraphy to date Greek inscriptions
F16.lineage: lineage and sequel: machine dating of ancient texts before and after Enoch

F17.quote: In addition, 11Q5 shows that in the late date range, a fairly certain style-based date estimate above 100 CE can also be achieved. This may go against historical reconstructions according to which the scrolls were hidden in the Qumran caves before the summer of 68 CE [ 40 ].
F17.claim: for 11Q5 the model gives a fairly certain date after 100 CE, against the reconstruction that the scrolls were hidden before summer 68 CE
F17.lineage: stated limits: radiocarbon superior, a first step, more research needed

F18.quote: Expert palaeographers among the article’s authors evaluated the style-based date predictions, condensing the prediction into two main categories: realistic and unrealistic
F18.claim: the post-hoc evaluation of the 135 predictions was made by palaeographers among the article's own authors
F18.lineage: accuracy and validation: errors of 27.9 to 30.7 years; 79% realistic on 135 undated scrolls

F19.quote: These are the first published results on date estimation for this collection of manuscripts. Future research, with more data and improved images, may be directed at further validation and refinement. … Now, Enoch shows that there is no temporal difference between the two halves of the manuscript
F19.claim: the first published date estimates for the collection, with further validation to come; for the Great Isaiah Scroll the two scribes' halves date to the same period
F19.lineage: stated limits: radiocarbon superior, a first step, more research needed

F20.quote: To our knowledge, Enoch is the first complete machine-learning-based model that employs raw image inputs to deliver probabilistic date predictions for handwritten manuscripts utilizing the probability distribution from 14 C output, and that is completed by palaeographic input while ensuring transparency and interpretability through its explainable design.
F20.claim: the study's claim of priority: the first complete machine-learning model giving probabilistic dates for handwritten manuscripts from raw images and radiocarbon distributions, with an explainable design
F20.lineage: what it offers palaeography: probability-based options, quantified objectivity, explainable design

F21.quote: This study in style-based date prediction using the Enoch approach is a first step. The advantage of the Enoch model is that it provides quantified objectivity to palaeography, reducing the method’s subjectivity and the role of tacit expert knowledge
F21.claim: a first step, whose advantage is quantified objectivity for palaeography
F21.lineage: what it offers palaeography: probability-based options, quantified objectivity, explainable design

F22.quote: It could be argued that the style-based predictions are influenced by the 14 C-based training of the model. However, the leave-one-out validation results indicate that unseen samples obtain their interpolated position on the time axis based on the detected handwriting style in the images.
F22.claim: the objection that the predictions only echo the radiocarbon training is met by leave-one-out validation
F22.lineage: accuracy and validation: errors of 27.9 to 30.7 years; 79% realistic on 135 undated scrolls

F23.quote: we have avoided using palaeographic estimates as target values for machine learning because our goal is to provide physical (material) and geometric (shape-based) evidences for manuscript dating
F23.claim: the model is not trained on palaeographic estimates
F23.lineage: the method: Bayesian ridge regression on writing-style features read from the ink trace, not the text

F24.quote: If palaeographers are willing to accept the use of ‘black box’, pre-trained deep-learning models that are based on completely extraneous large image and photograph collections, future research may be directed at adapting the output of such models
F24.claim: black-box pre-trained models are named as a future option that depends on palaeographers' acceptance, not as the method used
F24.lineage: what it offers palaeography: probability-based options, quantified objectivity, explainable design

F25.quote: First, 14 C date ranges and Enoch’s style-based estimates are overall older than previous palaeographic estimates. These older dates for the scrolls are realistic. … Second, ‘Herodian’ script emerged earlier than previously thought.
F25.claim: the radiocarbon and style-based dates are overall older and realistic; the Herodian script emerged earlier, beside the Hasmonaean
F25.lineage: the finding: dates older than the palaeographic estimates, a new chronology

F26.quote: Yet, the results of this study attest to the copying of multiple literary manuscripts before this period. One example is 4Q109, a copy of the biblical book of Ecclesiastes, a book which scholars tentatively date to the end of the third century BCE [ 15 ], for which Enoch gives a third-century BCE date prediction
F26.claim: literary manuscripts were copied before the Hasmonaean expansion; 4Q109, a copy of Ecclesiastes, gets a third-century BCE prediction from Enoch
F26.lineage: copying before the Hasmonaean expansion and before Qumran

F27.quote: Fourth, this study’s 14 C result for 4Q114 and Enoch’s date prediction for 4Q109 now establish these to be the first known fragments of a biblical book from the time of their presumed authors [ 15 ].
F27.claim: the radiocarbon result for 4Q114 and Enoch's prediction for 4Q109 make them the first known biblical fragments from the time of their presumed authors
F27.lineage: the key texts: 4Q114 by radiocarbon, 4Q109 by Enoch, copies from the time of their presumed authors

F28.quote: The results of this study thus dismantle unsubstantiated historical suppositions and chronological limitations, and call into question the validity of the default model’s relative typology. … More research is needed to solve this issue.
F28.claim: the results call the default relative typology into question; the Herodian-type dates challenge it, and more research is needed
F28.lineage: stated limits: radiocarbon superior, a first step, more research needed

F29.quote: This is an open access article distributed under the terms of the Creative Commons Attribution License … All data, code, and test film associated with this article are publicly available on Zenodo
F29.claim: the article is open access under the Creative Commons Attribution License; data, code and test film are on Zenodo

F30.claim: the study: Popović, Dhali, Schomaker, van der Plicht, Lund Rasmussen, La Nasa et al., PLOS One, published 4 June 2025, funded by the ERC (grant 640497, HandsandBible)

F31.quote: To overcome this problem, we present Enoch, an AI-based date-prediction model, trained on the basis of 24 14 C-dated scroll samples.
F31.claim: the NIH copy of the same article: the same definition (one work, one lineage with B1)
F31.lineage: what it is: an AI-based date-prediction model for the scrolls and the study that introduces it

F32.quote: 107 ( 79 % ) of the undated manuscripts were dated realistically and 28 unrealistic predictions ( 21 % ) were divided between too old ( 46 % ) and too young ( 39 % ), according to the palaeographers ( S7 Appendix ). With this sample size, the confidence margin is 7 % at α = 0.05 .
F32.claim: 107 of 135 (79%) realistic, 28 (21%) unrealistic, divided between too old and too young; a 7% margin (the figures the PLOS page's text drops)
F32.lineage: accuracy and validation: errors of 27.9 to 30.7 years; 79% realistic on 135 undated scrolls

F33.quote: 1 Qumran Institute, University of Groningen, Groningen, The Netherlands
F33.claim: the lead author's institute: the Qumran Institute, University of Groningen

F34.quote: Publishing in the journal PLOS One , an international research team proposes a new method for dating individual scrolls using artificial intelligence. According to the team, this analysis reveals that many of the scrolls are likely older than previously thought. However, not all scholars are convinced.
F34.claim: BAS: an international team proposes AI dating of individual scrolls; many scrolls likely older, by the team's account; not all scholars are convinced

F35.quote: Enoch examines the shapes of letters from the scrolls and cross-references the writing style with scrolls of similar style that have been dated with carbon-14 dating. In effect, the model performs its own comparative paleographic analysis.
F35.claim: BAS: Enoch compares letter shapes with radiocarbon-dated scrolls of similar style, in effect its own comparative palaeography
F35.lineage: the method: Bayesian ridge regression on writing-style features read from the ink trace, not the text

F36.quote: To train their model, the researchers performed radiocarbon analysis on two dozen scrolls, from four different sites in the Judean Desert .
F36.claim: BAS: radiocarbon analysis on two dozen scrolls from four Judean Desert sites trained the model
F36.lineage: the radiocarbon anchors: 30 manuscripts dated, 27 valid dates, 24 for training

F37.quote: Nearly all dates proposed by Enoch were significantly older than previous estimates. Notably, several texts commonly associated with the Qumran community were dated earlier than the site’s first period of settlement, showing that the scrolls must have originated elsewhere.
F37.claim: BAS: nearly all of Enoch's dates significantly older; texts associated with the Qumran community dated before the site's first settlement, so the scrolls originated elsewhere
F37.lineage: copying before the Hasmonaean expansion and before Qumran

F38.quote: “The results of this study are very interesting, and presumably important, but not earth-shattering,” … “Most of the conclusions of the study dovetail with what the great paleographers in the field, such as the late Frank Moore Cross , had already stated more than 60 years ago.”
F38.claim: Rollston (George Washington University): interesting, not earth-shattering; most conclusions dovetail with what Frank Moore Cross had stated sixty years earlier

F39.quote: “If anything, I think [the researchers’] work drew our attention to points we would have otherwise missed,” … “This is important evidence about the scripture scrolls and their character in the pre-Hasmonean period.”
F39.claim: Ben-Dov (Tel Aviv University): the work draws attention to missed points; 4Q52 and 4Q70 are evidence on scripture scrolls before the Hasmonaeans

F40.quote: “This is a way to move forward,” said Adler. … Here, there is an attempt to actually procure new data.”
F40.claim: Adler (Ariel University): a way forward, an attempt to procure new data

F41.quote: “Enoch’s calibrated date range for 4Q114 is: 230–160 BCE. … Thus, in this particular case, which is the one case where we can really fact-check Enoch, it is crystal clear that Enoch’s dates are much too high.”
F41.claim: Rollston: the 4Q114 range (230–160 BCE), which he calls Enoch's, is too high, since Daniel 7–12 cannot be dated before 167 BCE

F42.quote: “Overall, the scholarly community faces a serious question: Is this study reliable enough to substantiate a re-shuffle of the entire chronological paradigm of Qumran?”
F42.claim: Ben-Dov: whether the study is reliable enough to re-shuffle the chronology of Qumran is the open question

F43.quote: AI Dating of Scrolls: A new AI study suggests some Dead Sea Scrolls, including parts of the Book of Daniel, may be up to 100 years older than previously thought
F43.claim: the Reddit card (15 June 2025): some scrolls, parts of Daniel among them, may be up to 100 years older
F43.lineage: the magnitude in the press: 50 to 150 years, a century, up to 100 years

F44.quote: Researchers establish two biblical scroll fragments come from the time of their presumed authors.
F44.claim: JPost: two biblical fragments from the time of their presumed authors
F44.lineage: the key texts: 4Q114 by radiocarbon, 4Q109 by Enoch, copies from the time of their presumed authors

F45.quote: An artificial intelligence program named Enoch has advanced the dating of many of the Dead Sea Scrolls by 50 to 150 years earlier than previously believed, according to a new study published in the journal PLOS One.
F45.claim: JPost: Enoch moved the dates of many scrolls 50 to 150 years earlier, according to the study
F45.lineage: the magnitude in the press: 50 to 150 years, a century, up to 100 years

F46.quote: Researchers from the University of Groningen developed Enoch to analyze the handwriting styles of ancient manuscripts, combining radiocarbon dating and paleography to provide more accurate date estimates for individual Dead Sea Scrolls manuscripts.
F46.claim: JPost: Groningen researchers developed Enoch, combining radiocarbon dating and palaeography to date individual scrolls
F46.lineage: what it is: an AI-based date-prediction model for the scrolls and the study that introduces it

F47.quote: "With the Enoch tool we have opened a new door into the ancient world, like a time machine, that allows us to study the hands that wrote the Bible, especially now that we have established, for the first time, that two biblical scroll fragments come from the time of their presumed authors," the authors stated, according to Ars Technica.
F47.claim: the authors: Enoch opens the ancient world 'like a time machine', and two biblical fragments are from their presumed authors' time
F47.lineage: what it offers palaeography: probability-based options, quantified objectivity, explainable design

F48.quote: "In some cases we see dates that are 50 years older or maybe even a century older than previously assumed," Popović adds.
F48.claim: Popović: in some cases 50 years, or even a century, older
F48.lineage: the magnitude in the press: 50 to 150 years, a century, up to 100 years

F49.quote: The AI program analyzed the handwriting style of 135 scrolls with unknown dates spanning three centuries from around 200 BCE to 100 CE.
F49.claim: JPost: 135 undated scrolls analysed, spanning about 200 BCE to 100 CE
F49.lineage: accuracy and validation: errors of 27.9 to 30.7 years; 79% realistic on 135 undated scrolls

F50.quote: "Radiocarbon dating is a destructive method," said Professor Mladen Popović, an archaeologist at the University of Groningen and study lead author.
F50.claim: Popović, the lead author: radiocarbon dating destroys material, which the model is built to overcome
F50.lineage: the dating problem: palaeography without date-bearing manuscripts

F51.quote: Popović plans to apply the Enoch model to more Dead Sea Scrolls, as well as other ancient Aramaic texts like the Elephantine Papyri.
F51.claim: Popović plans to apply the model to more scrolls and to Aramaic texts such as the Elephantine Papyri
F51.lineage: lineage and sequel: machine dating of ancient texts before and after Enoch

F52.quote: "The advantage of the [AI] model is that it provides quantified objectivity to paleography, reducing the method's subjectivity," the authors write. The study suggests that scribes were copying multiple literary manuscripts before this period, which could have major implications for our historical narratives.
F52.claim: JPost quotes the authors' 'quantified objectivity' and reports copying before the period
F52.lineage: copying before the Hasmonaean expansion and before Qumran

F53.quote: From Ithaca to Judea Enoch is not the first artificial intelligence used to study ancient texts in general or the Dead Sea Scrolls specifically.
F53.claim: Haaretz's card: Enoch is not the first AI used on ancient texts or on the scrolls
F53.lineage: lineage and sequel: machine dating of ancient texts before and after Enoch

F57.quote: An international research team led by the University of Groningen has developed a new method to date individual Dead Sea scrolls more precisely by combining radiocarbon analysis with artificial intelligence-based handwriting analysis.
F57.claim: the ERC: a Groningen-led team's method dates individual scrolls more precisely, combining radiocarbon with AI handwriting analysis
F57.lineage: what it is: an AI-based date-prediction model for the scrolls and the study that introduces it

F58.quote: By analysing ink-trace patterns and character shapes using a neural network (BiNet), Enoch can predict manuscript dates with an uncertainty of around 30 years -more accurate than standalone radiocarbon dating in this period.
F58.claim: the ERC: Enoch predicts dates within about 30 years, more accurate than standalone radiocarbon dating in this period
F58.lineage: accuracy and validation: errors of 27.9 to 30.7 years; 79% realistic on 135 undated scrolls

F59.quote: Until now, dating has largely relied on palaeography, the study of ancient handwriting, which lacks a solid empirical foundation due to the absence of securely dated reference materials.
F59.claim: the ERC: palaeography lacks an empirical foundation for want of securely dated reference materials
F59.lineage: the dating problem: palaeography without date-bearing manuscripts

F60.quote: This provides, for the first time, a robust and objective framework for dating over a thousand manuscripts from the Dead Sea Scrolls collection.
F60.claim: the ERC: for the first time a robust, objective framework for dating over a thousand manuscripts
F60.lineage: what it offers palaeography: probability-based options, quantified objectivity, explainable design

F61.quote: The study also provides the first material evidence that two biblical scrolls, 4QDanielc and 4QQoheleta , originate from the same periods as their presumed authors in the second and third centuries BCE.
F61.claim: the ERC: 4QDaniel-c and 4QQohelet-a from the same periods as their presumed authors
F61.lineage: the key texts: 4Q114 by radiocarbon, 4Q109 by Enoch, copies from the time of their presumed authors

F62.quote: The Hands that Wrote the Bible: Digital Palaeography and Scribal Culture of the Dead Sea Scrolls … ERC-2014-STG 640497
F62.claim: the ERC project behind the study: The Hands that Wrote the Bible, starting grant 640497

F63.quote: The study also made use of an AI -based date-prediction model called "Enoch", which was trained by applying Bayesian ridge regression on the handwriting-style descriptors of 24 of the 14C-dated samples, for the paleographic dating of some 135 previously undated manuscripts.
F63.claim: Wikipedia: the 2025 study's AI date-prediction model 'Enoch', trained on 24 radiocarbon-dated samples, dated some 135 undated manuscripts
F63.lineage: what it is: an AI-based date-prediction model for the scrolls and the study that introduces it

F64.quote: The study found earlier dates and coexistence of the Herodian and Hasmonean scripts, into the 2nd and 3rd century BCE, and possible pre-Hasmonean evidence of scribal literacy.
F64.claim: Wikipedia: earlier dates, Herodian and Hasmonaean scripts side by side, possible pre-Hasmonaean scribal literacy
F64.lineage: the finding: dates older than the palaeographic estimates, a new chronology

F65.quote: This study proposes older dates for some of the scrolls. … The lead author is Mladen Popović from the University of Groningen in the Netherlands. … For example, the fragmentary scroll 4Q114 of the Book of Daniel is now dated to between 230 and 160 B.C.E., as much as 60 years earlier than previously thought.
F65.claim: Wikipedia: older dates for some scrolls; lead author Popović; 4Q114 now 230–160 BCE, up to 60 years earlier
F65.lineage: the key texts: 4Q114 by radiocarbon, 4Q109 by Enoch, copies from the time of their presumed authors
